#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(brms)
 
# Must match the folder name inside data/ (data/replication/).
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's.
experiment_id        <- "replication"

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# Bian, Leslie & Cimpian (2018), Experiment 1. Open data: Study1.csv from the authors'
# repository (https://osf.io/wnesy/). One row per referral: 691 referrals from 347 participants.
# The paper's 52.5% / 40.5% are model-based marginal means adjusted for participant gender and
# stereotype score; the raw proportions computed here are slightly different.
# Paper's key estimate: condition b = -0.483, 95% CrI [-0.807, -0.165].
orig_raw <- read_csv(file.path("..", "data", "original", "Study1.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
 
original <- orig_raw |>
  mutate(condition = if_else(brilliance == 1, "brilliance", "effort")) |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(n = n(), women = sum(nominated_woman),
            participants = n_distinct(subj), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("effort", "brilliance")))
 
original_p_effort     <- original$women[original$condition == "effort"] / original$n[original$condition == "effort"]
original_p_brilliance <- original$women[original$condition == "brilliance"] / original$n[original$condition == "brilliance"]
original_b <- c(est = -0.483, low = -0.807, high = -0.165)
```

## Guidance

One row per study for the key comparison: the original, your Phase 1 replication, and your
Phase 2 extension. The table fills itself in from the data as each phase is exported, using the
analysis code below (open "Show the analysis code"), which is shared by both phases so they are
analysed identically. Edit that code once, here, to match your design and preregistered

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

brilliance_items <- c("High IQ", "Superior reasoning skills", "Natural intelligence",
                      "Knack for big, bold ideas")
effort_items     <- c("Highly motivated", "Superior commitment", "Sustained dedication",
                      "Continual improvement")

# Counts how many items from a set appear in the selection text. Matches each item rather
# than splitting on commas, because "Knack for big, bold ideas" contains a comma.
count_items <- function(sel, items) {
  map_int(sel, function(s) if (is.na(s)) 0L else sum(str_detect(s, fixed(items))))
}

# Load one phase's data straight from the raw Qualtrics export (data/<id>/<id>_raw.csv) and
# apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that file is not there yet, which is how every
# section below skips itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  raw_path <- file.path("..", "data", id, paste0(id, "_raw.csv"))
  if (!file.exists(raw_path)) return(NULL)

  raw <- read_csv(raw_path, col_types = cols(.default = "c"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    slice(-(1:2)) |>                    # Qualtrics adds a question-text row and an ImportId row
    filter(Status == "IP Address")      # drops "Survey Preview" responses

  recode_cond <- function(x) if_else(x == "control", "effort", x)

  # One row per person
  participants <- raw |>
    transmute(
      participant_id = ResponseId,
      completed      = Finished == "True",
      condition      = recode_cond(condition),
      gender, ethnicity, residence, education,
      age            = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(age)),
      manipulation_check = memory_check,   # Qualtrics column name
      answered_randomly = str_detect(random, "^Yes") %in% TRUE,
      random_blank   = is.na(random),     # left the "answered randomly?" question empty
      n_referrals    = (!is.na(ref_gen_1)) + (!is.na(ref_gen_2)),
      same_referral  = same_referral == "TRUE"   # computed in anonymize.R, which drops the names
    )

  # One row per referral (each person made two)
  trials <- raw |>
    transmute(participant_id = ResponseId, condition = recode_cond(condition),
              ref_gen_1, ref_gen_2) |>
    pivot_longer(c(ref_gen_1, ref_gen_2), names_to = "trial", values_to = "referee_gender") |>
    transmute(participant_id, condition,
              trial = if_else(trial == "ref_gen_1", 1L, 2L),
              referee_gender,
              nominated_woman = case_when(referee_gender == "Female" ~ 1L,
                                          referee_gender == "Male"   ~ 0L,
                                          TRUE ~ NA_integer_))

  errors   <- tibble()
  complete <- participants |> filter(completed)

  # Exclusions: manipulation check (a) none of own-condition items, (b) any other-condition item;
  # not a US resident; under 18; reported answering randomly (or left that question blank);
  # no referrals; same referral twice.
  checked <- complete |>
    mutate(n_brilliance = count_items(manipulation_check, brilliance_items),
           n_effort     = count_items(manipulation_check, effort_items),
           n_own   = if_else(condition == "brilliance", n_brilliance, n_effort),
           n_other = if_else(condition == "brilliance", n_effort, n_brilliance),
           passed_manipulation_check = n_own >= 1 & n_other == 0)
  # Two analysis samples. Both exclude people who reported answering randomly.
  #   keep          : also requires passing the manipulation check (the original's rule)
  #   keep_no_check : does not use the manipulation check
  keep_no_check <- checked |>
    filter(residence == "United States", age >= 18,
           !answered_randomly, !random_blank, n_referrals >= 1, !(same_referral %in% TRUE))
  keep <- keep_no_check |> filter(passed_manipulation_check)

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, keep = keep, keep_no_check = keep_no_check,
       n_failed_manipulation_check = sum(!checked$passed_manipulation_check))
}

# Women referred and total referrals per condition, analysed participants only.
women_counts <- function(d, sample = "keep") {
  d$trials |>
    filter(participant_id %in% d[[sample]]$participant_id, !is.na(nominated_woman)) |>
    group_by(condition) |>
    summarise(women = sum(nominated_woman), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

# Rough stand-in (brilliance minus effort, % women referred) that ignores clustering of
# referrals within participants. The confirmatory model is the real key test.
diff_ci <- function(counts) {
  b <- counts[counts$condition == "brilliance", ]
  e <- counts[counts$condition == "effort", ]
  if (nrow(b) == 0 || nrow(e) == 0) return(NULL)
  pt <- prop.test(c(b$women, e$women), c(b$n, e$n), correct = FALSE)
  tibble(N = b$n + e$n, estimate = unname(pt$estimate[1] - pt$estimate[2]),
         ci_low = pt$conf.int[1], ci_high = pt$conf.int[2],
         statistic = unname(pt$statistic), p = pt$p.value)
}

# Side-by-side figure: any number of studies on the same axes, in the order given.
prop_ci <- function(x, n) {
  ci <- prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE)$conf.int
  tibble(p = x / n, low = ci[1], high = ci[2])
}
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y, condition = as.character(condition))) |>
    select(Study, condition, women, n) |>
    rowwise() |> mutate(prop_ci(women, n)) |> ungroup() |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           condition = factor(condition, levels = c("effort", "brilliance")),
           label = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = condition, y = p, fill = Study)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), position = dodge, width = 0.2) +
    geom_text(aes(y = 0.02, label = label), position = dodge, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "white") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = "Job description", y = "Referrals who were women", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Effect (brilliance − effort)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", `χ²(1)` = "", p = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Effect (brilliance − effort)` = sprintf("%.0f points", 100 * r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.0f, %.0f]", 100 * r$ci_low, 100 * r$ci_high),
         `χ²(1)` = sprintf("%.2f", r$statistic),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", diff_ci(original)),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: with manipulation check", if (have_data) diff_ci(women_counts(phase1))),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: without manipulation check", if (have_data) diff_ci(women_counts(phase1, "keep_no_check"))),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) diff_ci(women_counts(phase2)))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllr",
               caption = "Key comparison: difference in the percentage of referrals who were women, brilliance minus effort. N is referrals. This is a stand-in test that ignores clustering; the multilevel model below is the key test.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction
I will be replicating Experiment 1 of Bian et al. (2018), entitled "Evidence of bias against girls and women in contexts that emphasize intellectual ability." In this experiment, the authors tested whether describing a job as requiring brilliance produces gender bias in job referrals. Participants were asked to refer two acquaintances to a job described as requiring either "natural talent" and "intelligence" or "hard work" and "consistent effort." The authors found that women were less likely to be referred to a job when the job emphasized brilliance than effort. 

I chose this study because I'm working on an existing research project examining how "collective brilliance," the idea that brilliance is an inherent feature of a community, affects task performance. Our work has assumed that collective brilliance framing improves task performance relative to individual brilliance framing. However, it has focused on how people respond to brilliance messages about themselves. Bian et al. show that individual brilliance framing also shapes judgments about who belongs in a role. Replicating this study will establish whether individual brilliance framing produces bias in organizational referral context, and can provide a foundation for testing whether collective brilliance framing reduces that bias. 

The primary manipulation in this study is a text-based vignette describing a job opening at a company that either emphasizes intellectual ability or emphasizes motivation and effort. I will use the original descriptions from the supplementary materials. Participants will then complete a manipulation check and a referral measure in which they nominate acquaintances for the job and report each nominee's gender. Finally, they will complete a gender-brilliance stereotype measure and an open-ended justification of their referrals. The procedure described in the paper was clear and straightforward, so I don't foresee any significant challenges.

The key statistical test I will preregister is a multilevel mixed-effects logistic regression predicting nominee gender (0 = man, 1 = woman) from condition (effort vs. brilliance). The key test is the effect of condition on the gender of the job referee. 

A possible extension of this work is to examine whether race moderates the brilliance effect. The original paper reported only the gender breakdown of participants, so it remains unclear whether race shaped who got referred to jobs described as requiring brilliance. I would be interested in exploring whether participants tend to refer participants of their own race and if there is a pattern that emerges in who generally gets describes to jobs that require efforts versus those that require brilliance.


## Methods

### Power analysis

The original study found a small effect of approximately d = .213 (converted from the reported log-odds coefficient, b = -0.483, 95% CI [-0.807, -0.165]) with N = 347. Using the original proportions (40.5% vs. 52.5% female referrals), I conducted an a priori power analysis in G*Power 3.1 (Faul, et al., 2009) for an exact test of the difference between two independent proportions (α = .042, one-tailed, power = .802), which indicated a required sample of N = 458. Because of class budget constraints, I will use the original study's sample size of N = 347.


### Planned sample

I plan to recruit a sample of 347 US residents who are ages 18 or older on Prolific. The study uses a survey format on Qualtrics and corresponds to Experiment 1 in the original paper. Data collection will end once N = 347 participants complete the survey. There are open data associated with the original study, but this original study was not preregistered. The sampling frame for the current replication follows the same procedures from the original experiment without any additional preselection criteria. Estimated participation time is 5 minutes, with compensation set at $0.67 per participant (equivalent to $8.00 per hour), for a total projected cost of $307.67. 


### Materials

## Manipulation 

"Participants were asked to imagine that they are working for “a big company” that is 'looking to fill a couple of positions in their workforce.' They were then
randomly assigned to read one of two job descriptions. Participants in the experimental condition read a brief description that emphasized the candidates’ intellectual abilities.  In contrast, participants in the control condition read a job description that emphasized the candidates’ motivation, which is arguably a requirement for
most jobs (e.g., 'highly motivated,' 'superior commitment,' 'consistent effort'). This description was adapted from prior work (Bian et al., 2018), where it was found to
be gender-neutral (i.e., equally applicable to men and women)." 

This manipulation was followed precisely in the replicated study. 

## Manipulation check 
"Immediately after reading the job description, participants’ manipulation of it was tested. Specifically, participants were asked to check which attributes from a list of eight had been mentioned in the job description. Of the eight characteristics, four were relevant to the 'brilliance' job and four to the control job." 

Since only 2 traits were explicitly disclosed by the researchers in the original study ("high IQ" and "natural intelligence" from the experimental condition and "highly motivated" and "superior commitment" that corresponded with the control), I had to select the other 4 traits (2 from the "brilliance" condition and 2 from control) that were directly chosen from the manipulation text. 

## Referral measure
"Next, participants were asked to recommend someone they know who meets the requirements of the job, regardless of whether they already have a job. To mask the purpose of the study, we required participants to provide several pieces of information about the
person they were referring in addition to their gender (e.g., their first name, their age, their relationship to the participant). After completing this information, participants were asked to refer a second person and were reminded of the job
description before being allowed to do so." 

This measure was followed precisely in the replicated study.

## Additional measures 
Several additional measures were included in the original experiment, including a "brilliance stereotype" measure that explored preexisting gendered stereotypes, an "interest" measure that asked participants how likely they would be apply for the job themselves, and an open-ended response asking participants to provide justification for their referrals. 

These measures were excluded in the replication due to budget constraints and because they were not relevant to the main effect of interest. 


### Procedure

Participants began the study by completing a consent form and answering demographic questions (gender, age, ethnicity, country of residence, and education). The original study did not report which demographic questions were asked. Participants who did not reside in the United States or were under 18 were excluded. 

"Participants were asked to refer acquaintances for a job; half of the participants were told that the job was for brilliant individuals, while the other half were not. If there is gender bias in contexts where intellectual ability is salient, we should see that participants are less likely to refer women when they think the job requires brilliance." After participants were presented with the job description, they completed an attention check asking which traits were described. After completing the attention check, they were presented with the correct answers. 

For each referral, participants reported the referred person's gender, age, and relationship to the participant, along with a brief explanation for the referral.

Participants were then asked to report whether they answered the questions randomly and to share feedback before being presented with a debriefing form at the end. The entire study takes 5 minutes to complete. 

### Analysis plan
All analyses will follow procedures as closely aligned with the original article as possible. 

## Key analysis of interest  
Following the original study, referrals (0 = man, 1 = woman) were analyzed with a Bayesian multilevel logistic regression, with referrals nested within participants. 

## Exclusions 
Participants were excluded from analyses if they resided outside of the United states, reported during debriefing that they had not paid attention, or did not provide any referrals or provided the same referrals every time. "Participants were also excluded if they (a) selected none of the characteristics relevant to their condition, or (b) selected one or more characteristics relevant to the other condition (e.g., 'high IQ' in the control condition). 

### Differences from the original study

The primary differences between the original study and the planned replication are the recruitment platform and the measures collected. The original study recruited participants via Amazon Mechanical Turk, whereas the replication will recruit participants via Prolific. The original study did not balance participants by gender, but the replication did. The original study included both the referral measure and a brilliance stereotype measure, whereas the replication will include only the referral measure. As a result, the replication model will include two predictors (condition and participant gender) and their interaction, instead of the original three predictors (condition, participant gender, and stereotype score) with all two- and three-way interactions. In addition, the original study's estimated marginals means were adjusted for both participant gender and stereotype score; in the replication, they will be adjusted for participant gender only. 


| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample |U.S. adults on Amazon Mechanical Turk| U.S. adults recruited on Prolific | No. |
| Sample |U.S. adults on Amazon Mechanical Turk| Gendered balanced U.S. adults recruited on Prolific | No. |
| Setting | Online, unsupervised, on the participant's own computer | Online, unsupervised, on the participant's own computer | No. |
| Measures included | Referrals, stereotypes, interest, open-ended justifications | Referrals | Unlikely. The unstandardized coefficient may be slightly impacted without controlling for stereotype scores but not likely. |

## Pilot B
A pilot study was conducted on Prolific with 5 participants. The median completion time was 5 minutes. Participants received $0.67, which corresponds to $8.00 per hour. The original study did not report results with and without exclusions. I will report the key analysis both on the full sample and after applying the exclusion criteria because a high proportion of pilot participants failed the manipulation check. 

### Methods addendum (post data collection)

As planned, 347 participants were recruited from Prolific. Participants were excluded who returned to the survey after completing it once, reported answering randomly, failed the manipulation check, referred the same person twice, were under 18, or did not live in the United States. After these exclusions, 243 participants were retained, with n = 94 in the Brilliance condition and n = 130 in the control condition. Because the manipulation check led to high attrition, an exploratory analysis was conducted with participants (N = 330) who failed the manipulation check but met all other inclusion criteria. There were 164 participants in the brilliance condition and 166 in the control condition.

## Results

### Data preparation


### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data

# The same model is fit twice: on the sample that also excludes failures of the manipulation
# check, and on the sample that does not use it. Both exclude people who answered randomly.
fit_model <- function(keep_df, label, fit_file) {
  # 1. One row per referral, analysed participants only, with participant gender added
  model_dat <- trials |>
    filter(participant_id %in% keep_df$participant_id, !is.na(nominated_woman)) |>
    left_join(select(keep_df, participant_id, gender), by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(female       = case_when(str_starts(gender, "Woman") ~ 1,
                                    str_starts(gender, "Man")   ~ 0,
                                    TRUE ~ NA_real_),
           brilliance   = as.numeric(condition == "brilliance"),
           brilliance_c = brilliance - mean(brilliance),      # mean-centered, as in the original
           female_c     = female - mean(female, na.rm = TRUE))

  # 2. Same model as the original, without the stereotype predictor
  if (n_distinct(model_dat$brilliance) < 2 || n_distinct(na.omit(model_dat$female)) < 2) {
    message(label, ": model not run: need both conditions and both participant genders.")
    return(NULL)
  }
  dir.create("fits", showWarnings = FALSE)
  brm(nominated_woman ~ brilliance_c * female_c + (1 | participant_id),
      data = model_dat, family = bernoulli(),
      prior = set_prior("normal(0,1)", class = "b"),
      chains = 4, iter = 5000, warmup = 2500, control = list(adapt_delta = .99),
      seed = 251, file = fit_file, file_refit = "on_change",
      refresh = 0, silent = 2)
}

fit_with    <- fit_model(keep,          "With manipulation check",    "fits/phase1")
fit_without <- fit_model(keep_no_check, "Without manipulation check", "fits/phase1_no_check")

for (nm in c("With manipulation check", "Without manipulation check")) {
  f <- if (nm == "With manipulation check") fit_with else fit_without
  if (!is.null(f)) { cat("\n==== ", nm, " ====\n"); print(summary(f), digits = 3) }
}

# 3. Condition effect next to the original's
est_row <- function(f, study) {
  if (is.null(f)) return(NULL)
  est <- fixef(f)["brilliance_c", ]
  tibble(Study = study, b = est[["Estimate"]], `95% CrI low` = est[["Q2.5"]], `95% CrI high` = est[["Q97.5"]])
}
bind_rows(
  tibble(Study = "Original", b = original_b[["est"]],
         `95% CrI low` = original_b[["low"]], `95% CrI high` = original_b[["high"]]),
  est_row(fit_with,    "Phase 1: with manipulation check"),
  est_row(fit_without, "Phase 1: without manipulation check")
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Condition effect (brilliance vs. effort) on the log-odds of referring a woman.")
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare
the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and
does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or
a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both
informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
rep_counts          <- women_counts(phase1)                   # with manipulation check
rep_counts_no_check <- women_counts(phase1, "keep_no_check")  # without it
orig <- diff_ci(original)
repl <- diff_ci(rep_counts)
repl_no_check <- diff_ci(rep_counts_no_check)

if (!is.null(repl)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"),
            repl |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: with manipulation check"),
            repl_no_check |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: without manipulation check")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference (brilliance − effort)` = sprintf("%.0f points", 100 * estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.0f, %.0f]", 100 * ci_low, 100 * ci_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Raw difference in the percentage of referrals who were women (ignores clustering).")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need analysed participants in both conditions.")
}

```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(repl)) {
  excludes_zero <- repl$ci_low > 0 | repl$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= repl$ci_low & orig$estimate <= repl$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.0f points. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    100 * orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by
side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a
glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1. **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions,
   with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot
   them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.
2. **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open
   repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.
3. **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a
   screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out
   in columns:

   ````markdown
   ::: {layout-ncol=2}
   ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

   ```{{r}}
   # your replication plot here
   ```
   :::
   ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for
both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the
caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of referrals who were women in each job description condition, original study and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals that ignore clustering within participants."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original,
                `Phase 1: with manipulation check` = rep_counts,
                `Phase 1: without manipulation check` = rep_counts_no_check)
```

### Exploratory analyses

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Any follow-up analyses (optional). Label them clearly as exploratory: they were not planned, so
they generate hypotheses rather than test them.
:::

## Discussion


### Summary of replication attempt

Bian et al. (2018) Study 1 showed that women were referred less often in the brilliance condition than the control condition (b = -0.48, 95% CrI [-0.81, -0.17]). The replication partially replicated these findings. Women were referred less often under the brilliance condition in the same direction as the original, but the effect was about half the size (b = -0.20, 95% CrI [-0.60, 0.20]) with the manipulation check and b = -0.24, 95% CrI [-0.57, 0.08] without it. Since the replication intervals include zero and also the original estimate, the data are therefore consistent with a smaller effect or with no effect, and do not distinguish between them. 


### Commentary
Exploratory analyses showed that the brilliance effect did not differ by participant gender. There was, however, a main effect of gender, such that women were more likely to refer other women more often than men did, regardless of condition (b = 1.14, 95% CrI [0.75, 1.53] among participants who passed the manipulation check). Although we followed the original experimental paradigm closely, we observed a smaller effect in the same direction rather than the same effect. The sample also differed from the original. In the replication, participants were recruited on Prolific rather than Mechanical Turk and were gender balanced. There were no other differences between the studies that are likely to have influenced the results. The original authors were contacted about the high attrition from the manipulation check, but no response was received. 

:::

# Phase 2: Extension

**Track:** Best-practices rescue 

## Rationale
There are several possible reasons why Phase 1 did not reproduce the original result. First, the study was a single vignette study, which is often harder to replicate. Effects from a single study are often overestimated and tend to shrink on replication. Also, In the original study, additional participants were recruited so that 347 remained after exclusions fro the manipulation check. Because of budget constraints, we could not do this, so we recruited a fixed sample and applied exclusions afterward, leaving fewer analyzed participants (330 without the check and 224 with it) and wider intervals. Fourth, the original sample was collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk in 2018, whereas we used a gender-balanced Prolific sample in 2026. Participants today may be more aware of implicit stereotypes and more sensitive to small differences in wording, which could change how they respond. Because the estimate trended in the same direction but was smaller and less certain, we interpret the result as a partial replication rather than a failure. 


## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}

| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | U.S. adults on Prolific of any ethnicity; 330 analyzed participants (about 67% White, 22% Black | U.S. adults on Prolific who identify as Black or White; 164 analyzed participants (82 per condition) | Allows exploratory tests of whether the race of the participant related to who is referred, and whether the brilliance effect differs by race. |
| 2 | Instructions | The job description was shown on one screen | The description is shown one or two sentences at a time, and participants step through with a 5-secodn timer on each part | In Phase 1, 122 of 366 participants failed the manipulation check, mostly by ticking an item from teh wrong condition. Requiring participatns to read the whole description should raise the pass rate. |
| 3 | Trials | 2 referrals per participant | 4 referrals per participant | More referrals per person give more data from each participant, which reduces the number of participants needed for the same power. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
# Phase 2 sample plan: power to detect the ORIGINAL effect, with several referrals per person.
phase2_n_per_group   <- 82     # planned analysed participants per condition in Phase 2
referrals_per_person <- 4      # Phase 2 asks for more referrals than Phase 1's two
power_target         <- 0.80

# Within-person correlation of referrals: from the Phase 1 model if it was fit, else a default.
icc <- if (exists("fit_without") && !is.null(fit_without)) {
  sdp <- posterior_summary(fit_without, variable = "sd_participant_id__Intercept")[1, "Estimate"]
  sdp^2 / (sdp^2 + pi^2 / 3)
} else 0.01
design_effect <- 1 + (referrals_per_person - 1) * icc

# A. Sample needed for the target power. The test counts referrals, so convert to people.
n_refs_per_group <- ceiling(power.prop.test(p1 = original_p_effort, p2 = original_p_brilliance,
                                            power = power_target, sig.level = 0.05)$n)
n_people_per_group <- ceiling(n_refs_per_group * design_effect / referrals_per_person)
tibble(
  Quantity = c("Referrals per condition", "Referrals in total",
               sprintf("Participants per condition (%d referrals each)", referrals_per_person),
               "Participants in total"),
  Value = c(n_refs_per_group, 2 * n_refs_per_group, n_people_per_group, 2 * n_people_per_group)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
    "Sample for %.0f%% power to detect the original effect (%.1f%% vs %.1f%% women referred), two-sided alpha = .05, within-person correlation = %.3f.",
    100 * power_target, 100 * original_p_effort, 100 * original_p_brilliance, icc))

# B. Power at the planned sample, for three possible true effects.
power_people <- function(p1, p2, k, n_per_group) {
  power.prop.test(n = n_per_group * k / (1 + (k - 1) * icc), p1 = p1, p2 = p2, sig.level = 0.05)$power
}
p1_observed <- if (have_data) {
  rc <- women_counts(phase1, "keep_no_check")
  c(rc$women[rc$condition == "effort"] / rc$n[rc$condition == "effort"],
    rc$women[rc$condition == "brilliance"] / rc$n[rc$condition == "brilliance"])
}
effects <- tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.0f points", 100 * (original_p_effort - original_p_brilliance)),
                         "Half the original",
                         if (!is.null(p1_observed)) sprintf("Phase 1 (without check): %.0f points", 100 * (p1_observed[1] - p1_observed[2]))),
  p1 = c(original_p_effort, original_p_effort, p1_observed[1]),
  p2 = c(original_p_brilliance, original_p_effort - (original_p_effort - original_p_brilliance) / 2, p1_observed[2])
)
effects |>
  mutate(`Power, planned referrals per person` = scales::percent(pmap_dbl(list(p1, p2), ~ power_people(..1, ..2, referrals_per_person, phase2_n_per_group)), accuracy = 1),
         `Power, 2 referrals per person`       = scales::percent(pmap_dbl(list(p1, p2), ~ power_people(..1, ..2, 2, phase2_n_per_group)), accuracy = 1)) |>
  select(-p1, -p2) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power at %d analysed participants per condition, two-sided alpha = .05.", phase2_n_per_group))

# C. Expected precision of the brilliance effect (log-odds half-width), scaled from Phase 1.
if (exists("fit_without") && !is.null(fit_without)) {
  b1 <- fixef(fit_without)["brilliance_c", ]
  hw1 <- (b1[["Q97.5"]] - b1[["Q2.5"]]) / 2
  refs1 <- nobs(fit_without)
  refs2 <- 2 * phase2_n_per_group * referrals_per_person
  tibble(Study = c("Phase 1 (without manipulation check)", "Phase 2 (planned, expected)"),
         `Referrals analysed` = c(refs1, refs2),
         `95% CrI half-width (log-odds)` = round(c(hw1, hw1 * sqrt(refs1 / refs2)), 2)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Precision of the key estimate: Phase 2 is scaled from Phase 1 by the number of referrals.")
}
```

## Analysis plan
The confirmatory analysis for Phase 2 will be the same as Phase 1, with the key analysis of interest being the referrals that were analyzed with Bayesian multilevel regression analyses. The exclusion rule is unchanged from Phase 1. Participants are excluded if they do not reside in the United States, are under 18, report answering randomly, give no referrals or the same referral more than once, take the study more than once, or fail the manipulation check. The same model without the manipulation check exclusion will be reported as a secondary analysis. A pooled estimate across Phase 1 and Phase 2 will be reported as exploratory. 

Exploratory analyses will examine whether participant gender and race (Black vs. White) are related to who is referred, and whether the brilliance effect differs by gender or race. 

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}

              100 * p2_stats$estimate, 100 * p2_stats$ci_low, 100 * p2_stats$ci_high,
              p2_stats$statistic, p_text))
}
